procedural_history.originating_court: 2nd Additional District and Sessions Judge, Chitradurga (trial court) in Special Case (SC/ST) No. 1 of 2021.
procedural_history.impugned_order: Order dated 3rd September 2022, passed by the learned Single Judge of the High Court of Karnataka at Bengaluru in Criminal Petition No. 8468 of 2021.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The accused persons preferred a petition under Section 482 of Cr.P.C. before the High Court, praying for quashing of the proceedings pending before the trial court. The High Court allowed the petition and quashed the proceedings.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The original complainant, being aggrieved by the High Court's order, filed the present appeal (Criminal Appeal No. 1661 of 2024) before the Supreme Court.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court erred in quashing the criminal proceedings by exercising the powers under Section 482 of Cr.P.C in a complaint alleging offences under Sections 354D, 376(2)(n), 504 and 506 read with 34 of the Penal Code, 1860 and Sections 3(1)(r), 3(1)(s), 3(1)(w)(i), 3(2)(v) and 3(2)(v-a) of the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989.

facts: A criminal complaint was filed and a charge-sheet was submitted against the accused for offences under the Indian Penal Code (IPC) and the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989.
The accused persons filed a petition under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Cr.P.C.) before the High Court to quash these proceedings.
The High Court allowed the petition and quashed the criminal proceedings, citing insufficiency of evidence and material contradictions in the prosecutrix's statements.
The present matter is an appeal before the Supreme Court challenging the High Court's decision to quash the proceedings.
law: Section 482 of the Cr.P.C. grants High Courts the inherent power to quash criminal proceedings to prevent the abuse of the process of any court or to secure the ends of justice.
This power should be exercised very sparingly and with circumspection, only in the rarest of rare cases.
The Supreme Court, in the case of State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal, laid down illustrative categories where this power can be exercised.
One such category is where the allegations made in the FIR or complaint, even if taken at their face value, do not prima facie constitute any offence or make out a case against the accused.
application: The Supreme Court found no infirmity in the High Court's approach.
It held that even if the allegations in the FIR and the material relied upon by the prosecution were taken at face value, there were no sufficient grounds to proceed against the accused.
The Court determined that the case fell under the categories established in the Bhajan Lal case, which justify the quashing of proceedings.
The Supreme Court concluded that allowing the criminal proceedings to continue would amount to an abuse of the process of law and result in a miscarriage of justice.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appeal and upheld the High Court's decision to quash the criminal proceedings. It concluded that the High Court did not err in exercising its powers under Section 482 of the Cr.P.C. because, even accepting the prosecution's allegations as true, there was insufficient ground to proceed against the accused, and continuing the case would be an abuse of the legal process.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court erred in quashing the criminal proceedings by exercising the powers under Section 482 of Cr.P.C in a complaint alleging offences under Sections 354D, 376(2)(n), 504 and 506 read with 34 of the Penal Code, 1860 and Sections 3(1)(r), 3(1)(s), 3(1)(w)(i), 3(2)(v) and 3(2)(v-a) of the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989.
appellant_arguments: The provided text does not detail the specific arguments made by the appellant's counsel. It only states that the appellant (the original complainant) was 'aggrieved' by the High Court's order quashing the criminal proceedings and therefore filed the appeal.
respondent_arguments: The High Court correctly considered the material on record and concluded that the prosecution's case, even if taken at face value, does not constitute the ingredients of the offences charged.
Relying on Supreme Court precedents, the High Court rightly held that there was no material on record to constitute the offence of rape under Section 376 of the IPC.
Permitting the continuation of the criminal proceedings would amount to an abuse of the process of law and result in a miscarriage of justice.

cases.case_name: State of Haryana and Others v. Bhajan Lal and Others
cases.principle: For providing illustrative categories of cases where the inherent power under Section 482 of the CrPC could be exercised to prevent abuse of the process of any court or to secure the ends of justice.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The extraordinary power under Article 226 of the Constitution or the inherent powers under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure can be exercised either to prevent the abuse of the process of any court or otherwise to secure the ends of justice.
obiter: It is not possible to lay down any precise, clearly defined, and inflexible guidelines or rigid formulae, nor is it possible to provide an exhaustive list of the kinds of cases wherein such power should be exercised.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Supreme Court found that the High Court did not err in quashing the criminal proceedings, as even if the allegations made in the FIR and the material relied upon by the prosecution are taken at face value, there are no sufficient grounds for proceeding against the accused. The Court concluded that permitting the proceedings to continue would constitute an abuse of the process of law and result in a miscarriage of justice.
legal_tests_applied: The guidelines for exercising inherent powers under Section 482 of the Cr.P.C. as laid down in State of Haryana and Others v. Bhajan Lal and Others, specifically categories (1), (3), and (5).

Category (3): 'Where the uncontroverted allegations made in the FIR or complaint and the evidence collected in support of the same do not disclose the commission of any offence and make out a case against the accused.'

Category (5): 'Where the allegations made in the FIR or complaint are so absurd and inherently improbable on the basis of which no prudent person can ever reach a just conclusion that there is sufficient ground for proceeding against the accused.'
why_appellant_lost: Even when the allegations in the FIR and the prosecution's material were taken at face value, the court found there were no sufficient grounds for proceeding against the accused.
The case squarely fell under categories (1), (3), and (5) of the guidelines established in the Bhajan Lal case, which justify the quashing of proceedings.
The uncontroverted allegations and the evidence collected in their support did not disclose the commission of any offence or make out a case against the accused.

The allegations in the FIR were considered so absurd and inherently improbable that no prudent person could reach a just conclusion that there was sufficient ground for proceeding against the accused.
why_respondent_won: The High Court correctly held that permitting further proceedings to continue would be an abuse of the process of law and result in a miscarriage of justice.
The High Court correctly applied the established legal principles for exercising jurisdiction under Section 482 of the Cr.P.C. and reached a just finding.
The facts of the case fit within the illustrative categories laid down by the Supreme Court for when the power to quash criminal proceedings should be exercised.
policy_considerations: The inherent power under Section 482 of the Cr.P.C. should be exercised 'either to prevent abuse of the process of any court or otherwise to secure the ends of justice'.

While the power of quashing criminal proceedings should be exercised very sparingly and with circumspection, and only in the rarest of rare cases, it is necessary to prevent an abuse of process and a miscarriage of justice.
